ego.name: Benjamin Franklin
ego.summary: Benjamin Franklin was a Philadelphia printer, writer, inventor, scientist, civic organizer, diplomat, and statesman. His electrical experiments established his scientific reputation. His publishing, civic work, and diplomacy in France made him a leading figure in the American Enlightenment and the founding of the United States.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin's father was a Boston tallow chandler and soapmaker. Josiah financed two years of schooling and apprenticed Benjamin to James Franklin to learn printing.
connections.notes: Josiah's practical decision to place Benjamin in a printing apprenticeship shaped his early trade and education.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin's mother raised him in the large Boston household and was an early supporter of his career, though she disapproved of his Freemasonry.
connections.notes: Franklin described her as a discreet and virtuous woman.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin's older brother apprenticed him as a printer in 1718 and employed him on the New-England Courant. Their conflict over the apprenticeship contributed to Benjamin's 1723 departure for Philadelphia.
connections.notes: James was both a formative printing instructor and an early source of professional and personal conflict.

connections.relationship_description: Read entered a common-law marriage with Franklin in 1730 and managed the household during his absences. Her work helped sustain the Philadelphia home and business that Franklin repeatedly left for public service.
connections.notes: They remained partners until her death in 1774, although his prolonged residence in Europe strained the marriage.

connections.relationship_description: William was Franklin's illegitimate son, raised in the Franklin household by Deborah Read. Their later relationship was ruptured by William's Loyalism during the American Revolution.
connections.notes: The political split between father and son became one of Franklin's most painful family conflicts.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin and Deborah Read's son, known as Franky, died of smallpox in 1736 at age four.
connections.notes: His death was a major loss within the Franklin household.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin formed a Philadelphia printing partnership with Meredith in 1728, and together they became publishers of The Pennsylvania Gazette the following year.
connections.notes: The partnership helped establish Franklin as a successful printer and newspaper publisher.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin's only daughter frequently acted as his political hostess after Deborah Read's death and provided his Philadelphia household in his final years. Their relationship was at times emotionally strained, particularly during his years abroad.
connections.notes: Franklin lived with Sarah and her family after returning from France and left much of his estate to her and her husband.

connections.relationship_description: Bache married Franklin's daughter Sarah in 1767, initially over Franklin's objections because of Bache's financial instability. Franklin later accepted him and arranged his appointment as postmaster general to succeed him.
connections.notes: Bache and Sarah sheltered and supported Franklin in Philadelphia after the Revolution.

connections.relationship_description: Denham, an English merchant, helped Franklin return from London to Philadelphia in 1726 and employed him as a clerk, shopkeeper, and bookkeeper in his business.
connections.notes: Denham's help enabled Franklin's return to Philadelphia after William Keith's promises failed.

connections.relationship_description: Keimer was a Philadelphia printer and newspaper rival. Franklin took over Keimer's Universal Instructor, converted it into The Pennsylvania Gazette, and satirized Keimer through the fictional character Cretico.
connections.notes: Their rivalry formed part of Franklin's early effort to build a leading Philadelphia press.

connections.relationship_description: Bradford was a Philadelphia printer and publisher of The American Weekly Mercury. Franklin wrote the Busy-Body essays for Bradford's newspaper while competing with him in the city press market.
connections.notes: Franklin's early work for Bradford also gave him experience in adapting English literary journalism to colonial Philadelphia.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin maintained a long business relationship with Timothy, who successfully operated the South Carolina Gazette after her husband's death and continued Franklin's printing network in Charleston.
connections.notes: Their relationship extended across roughly three decades and linked Franklin's wider network of colonial printing partnerships.

connections.relationship_description: Hunter and Franklin were appointed deputy postmasters-general for British North America in 1753 and jointly oversaw the colonial postal system.
connections.notes: Franklin used the office to improve postal accounting and intercolonial communication routes.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin and Washington were leading figures in the Revolution and early republic. Franklin served as a Pennsylvania delegate at the Constitutional Convention that Washington presided over.
connections.notes: Their relationship joined Franklin's political and diplomatic experience to Washington's military and executive leadership.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin and Adams served together in the Continental Congress, supported American independence, and later joined the American delegation negotiating peace with Britain in 1783.
connections.notes: They differed in temperament and diplomatic outlook but worked together at crucial moments of the Revolution.

connections.relationship_description: Franklin and Jefferson served together on the Committee of Five that prepared the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and later shared responsibility for American diplomacy in Europe.
connections.notes: Franklin supported Jefferson's authorship of the Declaration while helping revise its draft.

connections.relationship_description: Jay and Franklin were fellow American peace commissioners in Paris and collaborated in the negotiations that produced the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognizing American independence.
connections.notes: Their work was part of the delegation's difficult effort to secure peace and favorable territorial and fishing terms from Britain.

connections.relationship_description: As king of France, Louis XVI backed the Franco-American alliance and French assistance that Franklin worked to secure as American minister to France during the Revolutionary War.
connections.notes: French aid, obtained through Franklin's diplomacy, was vital to the American war effort.

connections.relationship_description: Lee served with Franklin on the American diplomatic commission in Paris, where their cooperation was marred by deep personal and political distrust.
connections.notes: Their rivalry helped destabilize the American mission in France before Lee was recalled.

connections.relationship_description: Deane, Franklin, and Arthur Lee formed the American diplomatic delegation in France and signed the 1778 treaties of alliance and commerce with France.
connections.notes: Franklin and Deane worked within the same divided Paris commission during the effort to obtain French military and financial backing.

connections.relationship_description: As governor of Pennsylvania, Keith encouraged the young Franklin to go to London to obtain equipment for a Philadelphia newspaper, but failed to provide the promised financial backing.
connections.notes: Keith's broken promise left Franklin stranded in London, where he worked as a typesetter.

category_summaries.summary: Franklin grew up in a large Boston artisan household. Josiah Franklin's decision to place him in a printing apprenticeship gave him his trade. Deborah Read kept the Philadelphia household and business running during his absences. Sarah Franklin Bache's home became his domestic base after his return from France.

Printing gave Franklin a public voice in Philadelphia through The Pennsylvania Gazette. Partnerships, employers, rivals, and the colonial post taught him how to run businesses and communications networks. His work with printers from Philadelphia to Charleston extended his influence beyond one city.

Franklin's political circle carried him from the Continental Congress to diplomacy in Paris. Jefferson and Adams worked with him on independence, and Adams and Jay joined him in the 1783 peace negotiations. Lee and Deane shared the Paris commission that signed the 1778 treaties. French royal support supplied military and financial aid to the American cause.
